First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int {e}^{px+q}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{p}{e}^{px+q}+C
$$

We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{e}^{-4x-3}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}{e}^{-4x-3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-4x-3}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(-\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-4a-3}+\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-7}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{4{e}^{7}}-\frac{1}{4{e}^{3}}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-4a})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y={e}^{-4x}$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }{e}^{-4x}=\infty $

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{e}^{-4x}=0$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14037234/assets/dd3903454e30d878fee3cd1f58f3942db034fde534e514f99e2c14ddd892a9b3.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{e}^{-4x-3}\,\text{d}x & =(\frac{1}{4{e}^{7}}-\frac{1}{4{e}^{3}}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-4a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4{e}^{7}}-\frac{1}{4{e}^{3}}\cdot 0 \\  & =\frac{1}{4{e}^{7}}.\end{aligned}
$$
